paras: The lynching of John Skinner was the hanging of a Black prisoner by masked men who took him from the jail at Hopkinsville, Kentucky, early on Wednesday, March 14, 1888. Skinner was held on a charge of shooting Ballard Fourqurean the previous November, and the mob hanged him from a wild cherry tree near the spot of that shooting. A coroner's jury found death 'by parties unknown,' and the circuit judge directed the grand jury to indict the lynchers for murder.

The local Semi-Weekly South Kentuckian called him 'the notorious John Skinner, colored'; the Louisville Courier-Journal gave his name as John Henry Skinner, alias Cox, alias Reynolds. According to the South Kentuckian, he had confessed to the 'malicious and unprovoked' shooting, after which a posse hunted him for weeks. The Maysville Evening Bulletin wrote that because he faced only five years in the penitentiary, 'Fourquean's friends concluded they would take the law in their own hands.'

After midnight a body of masked men, probably one hundred by the local paper's estimate and one to two hundred by the Courier-Journal's, surrounded the courthouse and jail. Jailer George W. Long was seized at gunpoint and refused the keys, which the men found in his quarters; he was then made to unlock the jail. Six men entered the cell Skinner shared with three other Black prisoners, Bill Rawlins, Ed Vinson and Pig Green, who pointed him out.

Skinner asked to dress, and by the Courier-Journal's account said his death 'may be a source of blessing to you murderers.' With his hands tied by a leather strap and a rope around his neck, he was driven out the Cadiz turnpike about two and a half miles west of town, stood on a spring wagon beneath a wild cherry limb, and the wagon was pulled away. His body was found about 7 o'clock; Coroner Bell's jury found that he 'came to his death by hanging, by parties unknown,' by strangulation. Several hundred people viewed the body before burial in the Potters' field.

Two days later a badly spelled placard signed 'A Member of the Mob' appeared on the courthouse, justifying the deed as a necessity and hinting that prominent citizens had taken part. Judge Little of Owensboro, holding circuit court, instructed the grand jury to find the mob's members and indict them for murder. No report of indictments or a trial appears in the coverage.

Distant papers first ran a St. Louis dispatch of March 14 calling Skinner 'a noted desperado' who had tried to murder 'a peaceable farmer, B. R. Bourgenau'; it appeared the next day in the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer. Shorter versions ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and Wilmington's Daily Republican on March 15 and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on March 17.

A longer Hopkinsville special appeared in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette as 'An Incarnate Fiend' and in the Weekly Courier-Journal as 'A Hopkinsville Mob Rids the Community of a Brute With No Redeeming Qualities.' The Courier-Journal described an 'orderly mob,' judged that his death, 'though lynching is condemned, was a just fate,' and asserted that Black residents showed 'no sympathizers,' a claim with no Black source in the coverage. The Maysville Evening Bulletin headed its dispatch 'A Negro Desperado Hanged by a Mob,' and the Springfield Daily Republic wrote 'Lynched by an Orderly Mob.'

The South Kentuckian reported the hanging in detailed items and on March 23 insisted, against outside reports, that the tree was a wild cherry. Weekly digests carried condensed items into late March, with drifting details: Minnesota papers printed 'John Henry, alias Cox, alias Reynolds,' and the Stark County Democrat said Skinner had shot 'an inoffensive woman.'

Most dispatches placed the seizure at about half past one Wednesday morning, consistent with the local account, but the Maysville paper said 2 o'clock Wednesday afternoon and the Interior Journal 'Tuesday night.' Distances ranged from about a mile to four miles, though the local paper's two and a half miles on the Cadiz turnpike agrees with the Courier-Journal's two miles. The Maysville paper said Fourqurean's wound was one he 'cannot recover' from, while the Courier-Journal and South Kentuckian said he had recovered or was out.

reader.title: Lynching of John Skinner
bases: A mob of masked armed men took Skinner from the county jail and hanged him from a tree outside town (A10, A11, A16).

A mob of about 100 to 200 masked men seized Skinner, held on a shooting charge, from the jail over the jailer's refusal and hanged him; the coroner's jury found death 'by parties unknown' and the circuit judge called it a matter for murder indictments (A11, A16, A15). The placard and the Maysville account present it as punishment for his crime because the law's penalty was too light (A8, A15).
The local South Kentuckian, the Courier-Journal's Hopkinsville special, the St. Louis wire and the Maysville dispatch independently agree on the seizure and hanging (A11, A16, A3, A8).

accounts.label: Local paper (South Kentuckian)
accounts.gist: About 100 masked men took the keys from the jailer, removed Skinner from a shared cell and hanged him on the Cadiz turnpike two and a half miles west; a coroner's jury found death by parties unknown.

accounts.label: Courier-Journal Hopkinsville special
accounts.gist: An 'orderly mob' of 100 to 200 masked men with Winchesters seized the jailer and hanged Skinner two miles west on the Cadiz road near where he had shot Fourquean, who recovered; his death was 'a just fate'.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: At 1:30 a.m. a mob demanded Skinner, took the jail by force when refused, and hanged him on the Princeton pike four miles from the jail for trying to murder a farmer four months earlier.

accounts.label: Maysville dispatch
accounts.gist: Two hundred masked men lynched Skinner at 2 o'clock Wednesday afternoon because Fourquean's friends thought a five-year sentence too light.

accounts.label: Mob's claim (placard)
accounts.gist: A placard signed 'A Member of the Mob' justified the hanging as a necessity and warned evil-doers.

framing.detail: The Courier-Journal headlined 'A Hopkinsville Mob Rids the Community of a Brute With No Redeeming Qualities' and called his death 'a just fate' though 'lynching is condemned'.
The Maysville Evening Bulletin headlined 'Judge Lynch. A Negro Desperado Hanged' and called him 'a thoroughly bad character', giving the friends' reasoning without comment.
The local South Kentuckian gave a detailed factual account, called Skinner 'notorious', and later corrected outside reports about the tree.
The Springfield Daily Republic headlined 'Hanged on a Cherry Tree' and 'Lynched by an Orderly Mob', saying Skinner had 'wantonly and causelessly' shot his victim.
Distant papers ran the St. Louis wire ('a noted desperado', 'the wretch') or digest briefs.

conflicts.note: The local paper's account (body found about 7 a.m. Wednesday) and the Courier-Journal's March 14 special support early Wednesday morning.

John Skinner, colored, also given as John Henry Skinner, alias Cox, alias Reynolds; described as an escaped convict
